The VCSs procured during the initial DARHT construction project have accumulated an average of ten hydro detonations each, with an intended design life of ten. The VCS has advanced from a bare 6 ft. vessel to a state-of-the-art, multi-layered armor system that mitigates blast and fragment hazards to delicate detector systems from increasingly complex hydros, while enabling rapid turnaround for the next experiment. The knowledge gained from 16-plus years of vessel operations will be applied toward new VCS designs to yield an unrivaled set of imaging options while addressing VCS aging. Increasing the Quality and Quantity of Data Generated at DARHT Radiographic imaging capabilities have received modest improvements over the life of DARHT: two single-frame gamma ray camera (GRC) system upgrades have occurred on A1 while the original 4-frame GRC system is still operating on A2. More than 306 exquisite dynamic radiographic data sets have been collected with the two GRC systems over the last 23 years. Work is currently underway for the Advanced Sources and Detector (ASD)/Scorpius project on a host of GRC system upgrades, including Bucky grids, scintillators, and cameras that will be leveraged for advancements at DARHT. Imagery from A1 sets the standard for use by the weapon design community. In hydrodynamic test 3659, A1 was used alone to generate a high-quality case radiograph hinting at the future potential for combined case/gas-cavity (GC) experiments. Combining these two experiment types would reduce cost, eliminate variance, and shorten the weapon system development cycle time. The multi-pulse capability of A2 has proven the critical importance of time-resolved imaging, despite the performance limits of the machine when compared to A1. The combination of the two linear induction accelerators (LIAs) has provided rich three- dimensional (3D) data for the design community. Advancements to the A2 accelerator will restore and/or exceed the original design requirements and provide expanded beam tuning capabilities, which will enable increased quality and quantity of data generated from A2. Images from the cameras provide useful qualitative data for designers whereas radiographic analysis tools enable quantitative data analysis of the images. Advancements with radiographic analysis tools will establish the pathway to computed tomography. Techniques using physics-based machine learning (ML) methods are currently under development. These methods have already demonstrated 3D reconstructions of radiographs with limited views. While radiography is the primary diagnostic at DARHT, supporting diagnostics provide critical information to complete radiograph- ic data sets. Supporting diagnostics have advanced from film-based rotating mirror cameras and electrical pins to laser-based, fiber-optic diagnostics with velocity, position, and strain measurement capabilities.
